metadata.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Acute Spinal Cord Injury Patients
metadata.organization: AO Spine & Praxis Spinal Cord Institute
metadata.specialty: Spine surgery and spinal cord injury care
quality_flags: The referenced high-risk table and intraoperative checklist are not included.
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses surgical decompression timing and hemodynamic management after acute traumatic spinal cord injury, together with prevention and management of spinal cord injury during spine surgery. It also covers intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring and perioperative planning for patients at high risk of neurological deterioration. Its recommendations draw on topic-specific systematic reviews conducted using GRADE.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients undergoing spine surgery who are considered at high risk for intraoperative spinal cord neurological deterioration.
decision_rules: Identify patients at high risk before surgery, document their neurological examination using ASIA standards, and discuss informed consent.
After identifying a high-risk patient, convene a multidisciplinary discussion and plan an intraoperative protocol that includes IONM.
Before surgery, optimize preoperative factors, arrange intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, agree on an intraoperative management checklist, and secure a monitored postoperative bed.
For an unstable cervical spine or extrinsic cervical cord compression, plan fibreoptic intubation; also address patient positioning, MAP targets, and intraoperative imaging or image guidance.
During surgery, use the intraoperative management checklist.
After surgery, provide a monitored bed, document and repeat neurological examinations, address MAP parameters, and consider MPSS and advanced imaging with MRI.CT.

artifacts.title: AO SPINE PRAXIS CARE PATHWAY TO MANAGE PATIENTS AT HIGH RISK FOR INTRAOPERATIVE SPINAL CORD NEUROLOGICAL DETERIORATION
artifacts.description: Step 1: Identify patients at high risk using the referenced high-risk table, record a neurological examination according to ASIA standards, and discuss informed consent. Step 2: Hold a multidisciplinary planning discussion, optimize preoperative factors, arrange intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, agree on an intraoperative management checklist, and secure a monitored postoperative bed in an ICU or step-down unit. Step 3: Plan fibreoptic intubation for an unstable cervical spine or extrinsic cervical cord compression; plan to maintain MAP targets, use intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, position the patient, and use intraoperative imaging or image guidance. Step 4: Use the intraoperative checklist described as modified from Vitale et al 2014; its contents are not provided. Step 5: Provide a monitored bed, document and repeat neurological examinations, consider MPSS, address MAP parameters, and consider whether postoperative advanced imaging with MRI.CT is needed.
artifacts.summary: A sequential pathway covers assessment, planning, surgery, intraoperative management, and postoperative care for patients at high risk of neurological deterioration during spine surgery. It refers to a high-risk table and an intraoperative checklist whose contents are not included.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It organizes risk identification and coordinated perioperative measures intended to guide care for patients at high risk of intraoperative spinal cord neurological deterioration.

document_sections.heading: Guidelines Contributors:
document_sections.content: The AO Spine and Praxis Spinal Cord Institute guidelines provide evidence-based guidance for spine surgeons and multidisciplinary teams caring for people with acute spinal cord injury (SCI) worldwide. Their clinical topics are the timing of decompression after acute traumatic SCI, hemodynamic management after acute traumatic SCI, and management of intraoperative SCI. The guidelines identify current practices as well as knowledge gaps and implementation barriers that could inform further SCI research. Addressing those gaps is presented as important for improving care and outcomes. Each topic underwent a systematic literature review using the GRADE approach, and the evidence informed the recommendations. The reviews were published separately.

document_sections.heading: The Role and Timing of Surgical Decompression after Acute Traumatic SCI
document_sections.content: For adults with acute SCI, the guideline recommends offering early decompressive surgery, defined as ≤ 24 hours after injury, as an option regardless of neurological level. Quality of Evidence: Moderate. Strength of Recommendation: Strong. It does not make a recommendation for ultra-early surgery: the available studies were few, had small samples, used differing definitions of ultra-early surgery, and reported inconsistent neurological benefits.

document_sections.heading: The Hemodynamic Management of Acute Traumatic SCI
document_sections.content: To optimize spinal cord perfusion after acute traumatic SCI, the guideline suggests raising mean arterial blood pressure to at least 75–80 mmHg without exceeding 90–95 mmHg. Quality of Evidence: Very Low. Strength of Recommendation: Weak. It also suggests maintaining mean arterial pressure augmentation for 3–7 days for that purpose. Quality of Evidence: Very Low. Strength of Recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: The Use of Intraoperative Neuromonitoring and for the Use of Preoperative and Intraoperative Protocols for Patients Undergoing Spine Surgery
document_sections.content: For patients undergoing spine surgery who are considered high risk, the guideline recommends intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring. Quality of Evidence: Low. Strength of Recommendation: Strong.

document_sections.heading: TO MANAGE PATIENTS AT HIGH RISK FOR INTRAOPERATIVE SPINAL CORD NEUROLOGICAL DETERIORATION
document_sections.content: The AO SPINE PRAXIS CARE PATHWAY addresses patients at high risk of neurological deterioration of the spinal cord during surgery. The guideline suggests identifying patients at high risk for intraoperative SCI (ISCI) before surgery, discussing their management within a multidisciplinary team, and using an intraoperative protocol that includes IntraOperative NeuroMonitoring (IONM). Quality of Evidence: Very Low. Strength of Recommendation: Weak.

document_sections.heading: STEP 1: Initial clinical assessment
document_sections.content: Identify patients at high risk of intraoperative spinal cord neurological deterioration using the high-risk table. Record an accurate neurological examination according to ASIA standards and conduct a careful informed-consent discussion.

document_sections.heading: STEP 2: Preoperative planning
document_sections.content: Discuss the case with a multidisciplinary team, optimize preoperative factors, and arrange access to intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring. Agree on an intraoperative management checklist and ensure that a monitored postoperative bed is available in the ICU or a step-down unit.

document_sections.heading: STEP 3: Surgical/anaesthetic planning
document_sections.content: Plan fibreoptic intubation for an unstable cervical spine or extrinsic cervical cord compression. Maintain MAP targets, use intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, plan patient positioning, and arrange intraoperative imaging or image guidance.

document_sections.heading: STEP 4: Intraoperative management
document_sections.content: Use the intraoperative checklist adapted from Vitale et al 2014.

document_sections.heading: STEP 5: Postoperative management
document_sections.content: Provide a monitored bed. Document an accurate neurological examination and repeat neurological examinations serially. Consider pharmacological management with MPSS, attend to MAP parameters, and consider whether postoperative advanced imaging with MRI or CT is needed.
